item.title: Brand-New $299 Pokemon Release Confirmed for June 2027
item.description:
An all-new Pokemon release is set to launch in June 2027, but comes with a hefty $299 price tag. As the Pokemon franchise celebrates its 30th anniversary this year, fans have already been treated to major releases like Pokemon FireRed and LeafGreen ports for Nintendo Switch, and the highly acclaimed spin-off Pokemon Pokopia on the Switch 2. For Pokemon fans and collectors with a bit of extra money to spend, a new release brings home one of Pokemon 's most unique collaborations yet.

Add GameRant on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Pokemon has produced some wild collaborations over the past few years, ranging from McDonald's-themed Happy Meal toys to Target-exclusive apparel, and even Fender guitars. However, one of the most popular Pokemon collaborations to date is Project Voltage, which pairs the iconic creature-collecting franchise with Vocaloid singer Hatsune Miku across music, art, and collectibles. Project Voltage started back in 2023, and next year, fans can add a unique piece of the collab to their collection.

Pokemon Day and Night Officially Revealed

The Pokemon Company officially reveals a brand-new release called Pokemon Day and Night.

By Andrea Trama

Hatsune Miku and Meloetta Pokemon Figure Releases in June 2027

Figure manufacturer Kotobukiya is releasing an official Project Voltage figure featuring Hatsune Miku (Psychic) and Meloetta. The figure commemorates the first promotional art for the collaboration that portrayed Hatsune Miku as a Psychic-Type Pokemon trainer with the Mythical Pokemon Meloetta as her companion. Fans can pick up this figure at the Pokemon Center for $299, just over half the price of a Nintendo Switch 2 console.

  • Featuring virtual idol Hatsune Miku in her iconic Project Voltage Psychic-type ensemble
  • Manufacturer: Kotobukiya
  • Item Dimensions: 6 x 6.4 x 10 in
  • Materials: ABS / PVC
  • Item Weight: 1.1 lb
  • Price: $299.99
  • Release Date: June 2027

Sporting her iconic teal hair, Hatsune Miku transforms into a Psychic-Type Pokemon trainer in this Kotobukiya figure. Alongside the Vocaloid singer, the Mythical Meloetta appears in its Aria Form, where it is a Normal/Psychic type. Included with the figure is a stand featuring a music-note backdrop that helps display the three Poke Balls that Miku is tossing.

Two iconic game characters. One impossible mashup.

As part of Project Voltage, Miku received a new design and artwork featuring a Pokemon for all 18 types. This project kicked off with Miku and Meloetta on September 4, 2023 to represent the Psychic type, with other notable pieces featuring Miku with Pokemon like the Electric-type Rotom, Water-type Primarina, and Fairy-type Jigglypuff. So far, Kotobukiya and the Pokemon Center haven't confirmed whether figures based on Miku with the other 17 types will be produced.

The figure is currently sold out at the Pokemon Center, with no word on when a restock will happen.

If $300 is too steep a price for Pokemon fans to snag this Miku collab figure, there are plenty of other Pokemon collectibles releasing in the coming months that are a bit easier on the wallet. VIZ Media is releasing Vol 2 of Pokemon Adventures: Red & Blue Special Edition , a collection of the original Pokemon manga run for only $29.99 in April 2027. Additionally, an official Pokemon 30th anniversary art book series is releasing on December 18, giving fans a number of ways to celebrate the 30 years of the franchise.

item.title: Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake Is a Reminder of One Thing the Series Has Left Behind
item.description:
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time returned on Nintendo Switch 2, and I keep coming back to the ocarina. The remake brings back the songs that once let you interact with Hyrule in a way no other item could. This version even lets you hum a learned melody into the Switch 2 microphone and have Link play it in the game, which is awesome. The usual button controls are still there, but I like that Nintendo found a new way to use such an old idea.

Add GameRant on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Ocarina of Time also reminds me how much I miss playable music in Zelda. I really do like where the series has gone, especially the freedom of its newer games. Being able to approach a problem however you want is a huge part of their appeal. But I also used to enjoy learning a tune and keeping it in mind until I found somewhere to play it. There's something satisfying about making a song do something in the world, and the remake has made me want that back.

Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake Just Gave Elden Ring Something to Envy

Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is bringing back a feature Elden Ring still lacks, even though FromSoftware has already done it before.

By Josh Cotts

Ocarina of Time Made Music Part of the Game

In Ocarina of Time , songs weren't something you learned and forgot about. Epona's Song called your horse, while the Song of Storms brought rain when you needed it. Other melodies opened the way forward or helped me get around the map. They gave you a reason to lock in whenever someone taught Link a tune. Using the ocarina took a little more effort than selecting an ability, and that was part of the appeal. I was the one playing the notes, and I got to see the result.

—

Other Zelda games kept that idea going without simply copying the ocarina. Majora's Mask gave songs a major role in how you deal with time. The Wind Waker swapped the instrument for a conductor's baton, but music still had a purpose beyond the soundtrack. You didn't need to know anything about music to enjoy those moments. You just had to learn the melody and try it when the game gave you a reason to. Zelda lets you experiment with almost everything now, but it no longer lets you make music. Of all the things the older games have left behind, that's one I really want back.

Zelda lets you experiment with almost everything now, but it no longer lets you make music.

I'm a big fan of both Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom . They’re easily my favorite Zelda games, and possibly my favorite Switch games ever. I've spent hours wandering off course because something caught my eye, and I love finding my own way around a problem. I wouldn't trade that freedom for a return to the old formula. Still, I do feel the music is missing in these games. I know their quieter soundtracks are a deliberate choice, and that approach works for the worlds Nintendo built. But I miss the stronger melodies from earlier Zelda games. I can remember the old songs years later because I actually played them. I don't get that same connection from hearing a few piano notes as I walk across a field.

That doesn't mean the newer soundtracks are bad. Breath of the Wild uses its quieter music well, and Tears of the Kingdom has some brilliant musical moments. Nintendo has explained that it wanted sound to sit further in the background in these games. I understand the thinking, but listening is still different from playing. Breath of the Wild even has a musician whose songs lead you to secrets. Let me join in! The games let you do so much with your surroundings, yet music has become something you can only listen to.

The Ocarina of Time remake is a good reminder that an instrument can still feel at home in a modern Zelda game. The microphone feature is a small change, but it's the sort of change I really appreciate. You can sing a tune and hear Link play it back without having to memorize the button presses. Anyone who prefers the original controls can keep using them. I don't want the next Zelda game to recycle all of Ocarina of Time 's songs, though. The series has moved on, and its musical mechanics should move on with it. I'd rather have an instrument that fits the freedom Nintendo has spent years building into Zelda.

A song that changes the wind, for example, could have more than one use. You might play it to move a boat across the water, then discover that it also helps during a fight. Another tune could attract animals, with different results depending on where you play it. I'd enjoy figuring that out on my own rather than being told to use a specific song at a marked spot. Tears of the Kingdom already encourages you to mess around with the tools you're given. Music could work the same way. If Nintendo let you experiment with melodies instead of treating them as keys for particular locks, I'd spend a lot of time seeing what I could get away with.

Zelda Should Bring Back the Joy of Playing Music

I don't want the next Zelda game to play exactly like Ocarina of Time . I'm glad the series has changed, and Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom are two of my favorite examples of what it can do. There is room for playable music alongside that freedom. An instrument doesn't need to replace the newer abilities or slow the game down. It could just give you one more way to interact with Hyrule, and it's a way I've missed for years.

What to Read Next
5 Best Zelda Games to Play After Ocarina of Time Remake, Ranked
Take-Two Head Addresses Ocarina of Time and GTA 6 Competing
Zelda: Ocarina of Time is Already One of the Best-Selling Switch 2 Games

The remake has reminded me how fun it is to play a song and see the game respond. I want that feeling in a new Zelda game, with an instrument I can use because I'm curious about what will happen. Nintendo has done plenty to make Hyrule a place I can experiment in. Now I want to make music there again.

9 /10

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time

item.title: NVIDIA Potentially Made GPU More Expensive For Gamers By Funding AI Startups
item.description:
A new report has raised questions about whether NVIDIA helped keep GPU prices high by financing AI companies that purchased its chips, potentially allowing the semiconductor giant to clear excess inventory while artificially inflating demand. The allegations come amid mounting scrutiny of the semiconductor giant following the abrupt ouster of longtime NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang.

Add GameRant on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Huang's 33-year tenure at the company he co-founded came to an abrupt end on November 12, following revelations about multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected by U.S. authorities of working for Chinese intelligence and helping circumvent the ban on top-end chip sales to China. NVIDIA appointed longtime CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO while its board searches for a permanent successor. Previously little-known details about Huang's leadership and business practices have begun emerging in the aftermath.

NVIDIA CEO Resignation Will Have a Catastrophic Impact

The recent resignation of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is likely to have one of the biggest impacts on both the tech and gaming industries.

By Anthony Taormina

NVIDIA Allegedly Used Financing Deals to Sustain Demand for Its GPUs

In the latest example of that trend, a November 13 investigation by The Wall Street Journal revealed that NVIDIA had explored providing billions of dollars in financial guarantees to startups that otherwise could not afford its chips. The arrangements primarily targeted startups in the cloud provider space, as well as data center developers, trying to make long-term customers out of businesses with limited purchasing power. Some of the deals were spearheaded by NVIDIA Vice President Nico Caprez, Huang's son-in-law, who joined the company in early 2024 as a corporate development manager.

Two iconic game characters. One impossible mashup.
Can you name them both?

Caprez and fellow VP Raj Mirpuri reportedly began promoting these credit-support arrangements in spring 2026, attracting interest from dozens of companies. NVIDIA's backing allowed prospective customers to secure loans at favorable rates, while the chipmaker proposed receiving a share of their future revenue in return. The strategy raised (even) more questions about circular financing in the AI space and related industries, as the practice of a supplier effectively funding demand for its own products is not considered economically sustainable.

NVIDIA CEO Reportedly Feared an 'Avalanche' of Unsold AI Chips

The WSJ report also describes how Huang expressed concerns about NVIDIA's existing supply commitments during an August 2026 meeting with senior finance executives. Major cloud providers were exploring alternative processors, potentially reducing their reliance on NVIDIA just as enormous quantities of chip wafers and memory the company had committed to buying (largely from TSMC) were approaching delivery. Huang reportedly characterized the incoming supply as an "avalanche." This apparent risk of excess AI hardware commitments contrasts with conditions in the consumer market, where the RTX 5090 graphics cards and other modern GPUs had become increasingly difficult to find, partly because AI buyers were competing for available inventory.

NVIDIA's Financing Strategy Faced Internal Pushback

The financing plans faced resistance from Kress, with the now-interim-CEO questioning how NVIDIA selected borrowers, valued its guarantees, and calculated potential returns. During the August meeting, Huang reportedly disparaged her as "a deer in the headlights." Kress also helped reduce a proposed financial backstop for a major OpenAI data-center project in Ohio, with NVIDIA subsequently disclosing a $105 billion cap on its guarantee exposure. By late August, the company had paused some financing proposals and introduced greater executive and board oversight. Huang nevertheless continued emphasizing NVIDIA's pricing power, reportedly warning cloud customers in October against concentrating too much inventory among a small number of buyers. Meanwhile, growing AI infrastructure demand contributed to PC memory prices reaching new highs during 2026 as manufacturers prioritized more profitable server products.

NVIDIA Potentially Made GPU More Expensive For Gamers By Funding AI Startups
NVIDIA CEO Resignation Will Have a Catastrophic Impact
Nvidia CEO Has Resigned
Fallout: New Vegas RTX Available Now

Gaming GPU Prices Are Still Spiraling Out of Control as of Late 2026

Whether NVIDIA's financing arrangements indirectly made gaming GPUs more expensive is inconclusive as of yet. TechSpot's November 2 analysis found that graphics card prices rose approximately 35% between August and October 2026, based on a 10-country sample. In the U.S., the cheapest RTX 5080 was listed for $2,200 against a $999 launch MSRP, while the RTX 5090 reached $9,400 compared with its original $1,999 price.

item.title: Creature Collecting Game Officially Coming to Nintendo Switch 2
item.description:
A new creature-collecting game is officially making its way to the Nintendo Switch 2 , with Montabi set to receive a physical release on the platform. The new Switch 2 release combines elements of monster-catching, deck-building, and roguelikes for players to enjoy.

Add GameRant on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Monster-catching games have been a staple of the gaming industry since the Pokemon franchise first burst onto the scene in the late 1990s. The iconic monster-catching series from Game Freak sparked the rise of a multimedia empire that has become one of the biggest pop culture brands in the world, including the Pokemon video games, the Pokemon TCG , and a wealth of merchandise. Pokemon 's success has inspired plenty of other creators to bring their own spin to monster-catching games, both with indie games like Temtem and Cassette Beasts and AAA games like Dragon Quest Monsters . Now, a cute and complex monster-catching game on Switch 2 is getting a new release.

Brand-New Switch 2 JRPG Just Gave Stardew Valley and Pokemon Fans Another Great Option

A new Switch 2 RPG offers something for Stardew Valley and Pokemon fans, but its most interesting feature goes beyond either game's usual formula.

By Rain Egan

Creature-Collecting Game Montabi Gets Physical Switch 2 Release

item.title: 8 NES Games By Nintendo That Are Forgotten Masterpieces
item.description:
Nintendo's NES library is usually remembered through blockbusters like Super Mario Bros. and The Legend of Zelda . I know I’m guilty of that, for sure. Those games definitely earned their status, but I’ve found myself thinking about Nintendo's bolder 8-bit ideas that just faded into the background. I love digging through that part of its catalog because the games are often stranger than the famous ones. Some take familiar genres somewhere unexpected, while others build an entire game around a control scheme that nobody tried again.

Add GameRant on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

These seven Nintendo-made NES games deserve another look. They don't all have the same reputation: Kid Icarus and Balloon Fight still have recognizable names, while Gumshoe and Devil World remain deep cuts. Several are included in Nintendo Switch Online's NES collection, making them easier to revisit than a lot of retro curiosities. I've ranked them by how much fun their ideas still offer and how badly they deserve more attention.

8 Clu Clu Land (1984)

A Maze Game Where Turning Is the Challenge

Most maze games let you turn whenever you want. Clu Clu Land, not so much. Bubbles keeps moving, and you steer by grabbing poles to swing around them. The goal is to reveal hidden gold bars, which form pictures once you've traced the right paths. Every turn feels like a tiny physics problem, especially when you're used to rushing to finish a stage.

More Games

The challenge itself comes from learning the movement instead of memorizing corridors. Sea urchins keep the pressure up, and Bubbles can stun them with an electric attack. Two-player co-op makes the awkward controls a shared problem, usually with hilarious results. It takes practice to get comfortable, but the moment the movement clicks is enormously satisfying.

7 Devil World (1984)

The Maze Itself Wants You Gone

At first glance, Devil World looks like Nintendo's answer to Pac-Man . Tamagon, a little green dragon, moves through corridors collecting items and avoiding enemies. Then the devil at the top of the screen points in a direction, and the entire maze starts scrolling. Suddenly, the walls are as dangerous as anything chasing you, turning a simple idea into a frantic test of awareness.

5 NES Games That Basically Aged Like Fine Wine

Most NES games have aged like milk in the hot sun, but a few exceptions exist. Mainly, these classics are still near-perfect today.

By Mark Sammut

That constant movement forces quick decisions, especially when a corridor starts closing around Tamagon. Crosses let him breathe fire, giving you a way to fight back while navigating the shifting maze. The game's religious imagery kept it out of the original North American NES lineup given the climate at the time, which helps explain its obscurity. Still, I find its central gimmick more memorable than plenty of better-known arcade games.

6 Gumshoe (1986)

A Light-Gun Platformer That Breaks Every Rule

Few NES games are as wonderfully strange as Gumshoe . Detective Mr. Stevenson runs automatically, and the NES Zapper does the work. Shoot Stevenson and he jumps; fire elsewhere to take out enemies or clear hazards. Nintendo turned a peripheral best known for Duck Hunt into the control scheme for a full platforming game, and the result is charmingly chaotic.

I admire how fully Gumshoe commits to the idea. You're managing ammunition and timing every shot while searching for the diamonds needed to rescue Stevenson's kidnapped daughter. It demands far more precision than its odd premise suggests. Because the original Zapper depends on CRT technology, the game is difficult to revisit on modern displays. That's a frustrating fate for something this inventive.

5 Balloon Fight (1985)

Floaty Controls Make Every Match Unpredictable

Balloon Fight has an immediately charming setup. You flap to gain height, drift with momentum, and try to land on an opponent's balloons before they pop yours. The rules take seconds to understand, but controlling your movement demands concentration. Every panicked correction sends you somewhere new, often straight into the enemy you were trying to avoid.

5 Classic NES Games That Hold Up As 10/10 Masterpieces

Most NES games are easy to appreciate but hard to love, but these masterpeices have stood the test of time so well that they still feel perfect.

13
By Mark Sammut

That unpredictability is why I rate it so highly. Downed rivals can recover if you don't finish them, while lightning and a hungry fish make staying airborne a balancing act. Two-player sessions regularly become accidental battles, and the endless “Balloon Trip” mode strips everything down to movement mastery. It's the sort of arcade game that turns a five-minute break into another dozen attempts.

4 Wrecking Crew (1985)

Mario Trades Jumping for Clever Demolition Puzzles

Wrecking Crew gives Mario one of his strangest jobs: a demolition worker armed with a hammer and no ability to jump. I suppose it’s not too far from plumbing. The objective is to smash designated walls and structures, but breaking everything in sight is a terrible strategy. Destroy the wrong object, and you've blocked a route or trapped yourself. Every level asks you to think before you swing.

The stages work as compact logic puzzles, with enemies such as Foreman Spike disrupting your plans. Better still, there's a level editor, an ambitious addition to a 1985 NES release, even though saving creations originally required extra hardware. I enjoy seeing Mario in a game that rewards patience over reflexes — I think that's a theme in a lot of these entries. His early puzzle-platforming career deserves far more appreciation.

3 Kid Icarus (1986)

Pit Had a Fascinating Story Before Smash Bros.

Pit gets plenty of recognition through Super Smash Bros. , but his first adventure remains a bit of an oddity. Kid Icarus combines vertical climbing with side-scrolling stages and fortress-like labyrinths. You collect hearts to spend in shops, improve Pit's strength, and work toward defeating Medusa to rescue Palutena. It's brutally difficult at the start, before your upgrades start making a difference.

8 Best Fantasy Games Of The 80s, Ranked

The 1980s saw the birth of several iconic fantasy video game IPs that continue to dominate the genre to this day.

4
By Ollie Tuscarny

The gradual increase in health and equipment gives the whole game a rewarding sense of progression. Each section asks for a different skill, from careful climbing to figuring out a fortress's layout. There's an ambitious action-platformer beneath the rough edges, and the original game deserves recognition for its design rather than simply being remembered as Pit's debut.

2 Zoda's Revenge: StarTropics 2 (1994)

A Late NES Sequel With Smoother Action

Zoda's Revenge: StarTropics 2 arrived in 1994, when the SNES had already taken center stage. The timing buried a sequel that made some smart improvements. Mike Jones returns, but the tropical islands give way to a journey through history, with stops involving Cleopatra and Leonardo da Vinci. It's an unexpectedly playful direction for Nintendo's overlooked adventure series.

The biggest upgrade is movement: Mike can travel and attack diagonally, making fights feel less rigid than in the original. I love the historical detours, even if they sacrifice some of the first game's distinctive island atmosphere. As the final original entry in the series, Zoda's Revenge shows how much a late-generation NES game could refine a promising formula.

1 StarTropics (1990)

Nintendo’s Forgotten Adventure Series Deserved Better

Of everything here, StarTropics is the game I'd most like Nintendo to revisit. Mike Jones arrives on a tropical island and discovers that his archaeologist uncle has disappeared. What follows is a cheerful, mysterious rescue mission that trades The Legend of Zelda 's fantasy world for island villages, submarine travel, and dangerous dungeons. Its setting gives the adventure a personality all its own.

10 Near-Perfect 1990s Video Games That No One Remembers

The 1990s was a wonderful era for games, but some great examples have been forgotten.

1
By Chris Littlechild

The yo-yo combat and grid-based movement have their quirks, but the mix of exploration and puzzles makes StarTropics special. My favorite detail is the letter that was included with the original cartridge: players had to dip it in water to uncover a code needed in the game. I'm a little young to remember that exact experience, but I still like the idea. That bizarre, brilliant puzzle captures the creativity of Nintendo's forgotten NES experiments, and it's why this takes my top spot.
